claim: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is one of the leading approaches to non-invasively treat a variety of brain disorders.
source: One of the leading approaches to non-invasively treat a variety of brain disorders is transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).
evidence: This is a general statement about TMS's clinical use, supported by established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Very little is known about the action of TMS at the cellular level.
source: However, despite its clinical prevalence, very little is known about the action of TMS at the cellular level let alone what effect it might have at the subcellular level (e.g. dendrites).
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study, based on the authors' assessment of existing literature.

claim: TMS causes GABAB-mediated inhibition of sensory-evoked dendritic Ca2+ activity in layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: We find that TMS causes GABAB-mediated inhibition of sensory-evoked dendritic Ca2+ activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including pharmacological blockade experiments with CGP52432.

claim: TMS directly activates fibers within the upper cortical layers.
source: We conclude that TMS directly activates fibers within the upper cortical layers that leads to the activation of dendrite-targeting inhibitory neurons which in turn suppress dendritic Ca2+ activity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental observations showing TMS-evoked activity in upper layers and the effects of blocking excitatory transmission.

claim: TMS leads to the activation of dendrite-targeting inhibitory neurons.
source: We conclude that TMS directly activates fibers within the upper cortical layers that leads to the activation of dendrite-targeting inhibitory neurons which in turn suppress dendritic Ca2+ activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing GABA-mediated inhibition and the laminar profile of TMS effects.

claim: TMS can be used to both enhance and impair cognitive abilities.
source: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) holds great promise as a non-invasive method that can be used to both enhance and impair cognitive abilities (Eldaief et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TMS has proved to be an important tool for addressing basic questions about brain function as well as for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes.
source: As such, it has proved to be an important tool for addressing basic questions about brain function as well as for diagnostic and therapeutic purposes (Fregni and Pascual-Leone, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TMS affects the action of feedback projections.
source: As a general rule, TMS affects the action of feedback projections (Juan and Walsh, 2003; Hung et al., 2005; Camprodon et al., 2010; Zanto et al., 2011) leading to a disruption in perception (Shimojo et al., 2001; Kammer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: TMS leads to a disruption in perception.
source: As a general rule, TMS affects the action of feedback projections (Juan and Walsh, 2003; Hung et al., 2005; Camprodon et al., 2010; Zanto et al., 2011) leading to a disruption in perception (Shimojo et al., 2001; Kammer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TMS has been used as a therapeutic method to alleviate some of the symptoms of hemispatial neglect.
source: but it has also been used as a therapeutic method to alleviate some of the symptoms of hemispatial neglect (Nyffeler et al., 2009), schizophrenia including auditory hallucinations (Giesel et al., 2012), pain, depression and epilepsy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: TMS has been used as a therapeutic method to alleviate symptoms of schizophrenia including auditory hallucinations.
source: but it has also been used as a therapeutic method to alleviate some of the symptoms of hemispatial neglect (Nyffeler et al., 2009), schizophrenia including auditory hallucinations (Giesel et al., 2012), pain, depression and epilepsy.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The precise effects of TMS at the level of a single neuron are very difficult to gauge, particularly in humans.
source: Despite great interest (Mueller et al., 2014), the cellular influence of TMS has yet to be ascertained since the precise effects of TMS at the level of a single neuron are very difficult to gauge, particularly in humans.
evidence: This statement reflects the technical challenges in the field, supported by citation and general knowledge.

claim: Dendrites can shape synaptic input to be greater or less than their linear sum.
source: Since dendrites can shape synaptic input to be greater or less than their linear sum (Polsky et al., 2004; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Larkum et al., 2009) thereby altering the firing properties of the neuron (Larkum et al., 1999), the active properties of dendrites have attracted attention and have been linked to cognitive processes and feature selectivity (Lavzin et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Dendritic properties can alter the firing properties of the neuron.
source: Since dendrites can shape synaptic input to be greater or less than their linear sum (Polsky et al., 2004; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Larkum et al., 2009) thereby altering the firing properties of the neuron (Larkum et al., 1999), the active properties of dendrites have attracted attention and have been linked to cognitive processes and feature selectivity (Lavzin et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Active properties of dendrites have been linked to cognitive processes and feature selectivity.
source: Since dendrites can shape synaptic input to be greater or less than their linear sum (Polsky et al., 2004; Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Larkum et al., 2009) thereby altering the firing properties of the neuron (Larkum et al., 1999), the active properties of dendrites have attracted attention and have been linked to cognitive processes and feature selectivity (Lavzin et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2012; Smith et al., 2013; Cichon and Gan, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Active dendritic processing underlies a general principle of cortical operation that facilitates parallel associations between different cortical regions and the thalamus.
source: Furthermore, it has been suggested that active dendritic processing underlies a more general principle of cortical operation that facilitates parallel associations between different cortical regions and the thalamus (Larkum, 2013) which is controlled by dendritic inhibition (Palmer et al., 2012; Lovett-Barron and Losonczy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work and is presented as a hypothesis.

claim: Dendritic inhibition controls the principle of cortical operation involving parallel associations.
source: Furthermore, it has been suggested that active dendritic processing underlies a more general principle of cortical operation that facilitates parallel associations between different cortical regions and the thalamus (Larkum, 2013) which is controlled by dendritic inhibition (Palmer et al., 2012; Lovett-Barron and Losonczy, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TMS caused a significant decrease in the hindpaw-evoked dendritic Ca2+ response when triggered 50 ms before hindpaw stimulation.
source: TMS caused a significant decrease in the hindpaw-evoked dendritic Ca2+ response when triggered 50 ms before hindpaw stimulation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), both in the maximum amplitude (control, 7.3 ± 1.5 △F/F versus TMS, 5.0 ± 1.1 △F/F, n = 17, p<0.05) and integral (control, 4.3 ± 0.9 △F/F•s versus TMS, 2.4 ± 0.6 △F/F•s; n = 17; p<0.001, Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance reported.

claim: The size of the coil did not influence the TMS inhibition results.
source: Further, the size of the coil (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and the type of hindpaw stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) did not influence the results, whereas the distance of the coil from the cortical region of interest influenced the effectiveness of the TMS inhibition on the dendritic sensory responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The type of hindpaw stimulation did not influence the TMS inhibition results.
source: Further, the size of the coil (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and the type of hindpaw stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) did not influence the results, whereas the distance of the coil from the cortical region of interest influenced the effectiveness of the TMS inhibition on the dendritic sensory responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The distance of the coil from the cortical region of interest influenced the effectiveness of the TMS inhibition on the dendritic sensory responses.
source: Further, the size of the coil (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and the type of hindpaw stimulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) did not influence the results, whereas the distance of the coil from the cortical region of interest influenced the effectiveness of the TMS inhibition on the dendritic sensory responses (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites are strongly inhibited by the activation of post-synaptic GABAB receptors.
source: L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites have been previously shown to be strongly inhibited by the activation of post-synaptic GABAB (Pérez-Garci et al., 2006; Chalifoux and Carter, 2011; Palmer et al., 2012) receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blocking GABAB receptors prevented the TMS-evoked decrease in the Ca2+ response to hindpaw stimulation.
source: Blocking GABAB receptors prevented the TMS-evoked decrease in the Ca2+ response to hindpaw stimulation in both the integral (controlcgp, 2.3 ± 0.5 △F/F•s versus TMScgp, 2.1 ± 0.5 △F/F•s; p=0.62) and maximum amplitude (controlcgp, 7.7 ± 2.8 △F/F versus TMScgp, 7.2 ± 1.9 △F/F; n = 7; p=0.66, Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: L5 dendrites are inhibited by the activation of GABAA receptors.
source: L5 dendrites have been shown to also be inhibited by the activation of GABAA (Kim et al., 1995; Murayama et al., 2009) receptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Cortical application of Gabazine causes a six-fold increase in the sensory evoked dendritic response.
source: Although cortical application of Gabazine causes a six-fold increase in the sensory evoked dendritic response (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), block of GABAA receptors also prevented the TMS-evoked decrease in Ca2+ response to hindpaw stimulation (HS amplitude, 130 ± 30% of control; n = 6; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Block of GABAA receptors prevented the TMS-evoked decrease in Ca2+ response to hindpaw stimulation.
source: Although cortical application of Gabazine causes a six-fold increase in the sensory evoked dendritic response (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), block of GABAA receptors also prevented the TMS-evoked decrease in Ca2+ response to hindpaw stimulation (HS amplitude, 130 ± 30% of control; n = 6; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: TMS itself did not directly activate L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites.
source: TMS itself did not directly activate L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites (Figure 3A; n = 4), contrasting greatly to the large TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in cells within layer 2/3 (L2/3; 3.0 ± 1.1 △F/F; n = 3; Figure 3B) and layer 1 (L1; 5.5 ± 2.1 △F/F; n = 12; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing no Ca2+ response in L5 dendrites to TMS alone.

claim: TMS evoked a large Ca2+ response in cells within layer 2/3.
source: TMS itself did not directly activate L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites (Figure 3A; n = 4), contrasting greatly to the large TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in cells within layer 2/3 (L2/3; 3.0 ± 1.1 △F/F; n = 3; Figure 3B) and layer 1 (L1; 5.5 ± 2.1 △F/F; n = 12; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Ca2+ responses in upper layers.

claim: TMS evoked a large Ca2+ response in cells within layer 1.
source: TMS itself did not directly activate L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites (Figure 3A; n = 4), contrasting greatly to the large TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in cells within layer 2/3 (L2/3; 3.0 ± 1.1 △F/F; n = 3; Figure 3B) and layer 1 (L1; 5.5 ± 2.1 △F/F; n = 12; Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing Ca2+ responses in upper layers.

claim: The TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in upper cortical layers was similar to the response evoked by physiological stimulation via hindpaw stimulation.
source: Importantly, the TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in these upper cortical layers was similar to the response evoked by physiological stimulation via hindpaw stimulation (L2/3, 3.5 ± 1.2 △F/F•s and L1, 6.4 ± 2 △F/F•s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing TMS and hindpaw stimulation responses.

claim: The lack of a direct response to TMS in L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites implies that the inhibition of sensory evoked dendritic transients was mediated by the action of inhibitory neurons.
source: The lack of a direct response to TMS in L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites implies that the inhibition of sensory evoked dendritic transients was mediated by the action of inhibitory neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that TMS does not directly activate L5 dendrites.

claim: CNQX prevented the inhibitory effect of TMS in L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites.
source: Under these conditions, CNQX prevented the inhibitory effect of TMS in L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites (n = 10; Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that blocking AMPA receptors abolishes TMS inhibition.

claim: TMS-evoked inhibition in L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites is of polysynaptic (indirect) origin.
source: Therefore, since blocking excitatory AMPA-mediated transmission prevented the TMS inhibitory effect, TMS-evoked inhibition in L5 pyramidal neuron dendrites must be of polysynaptic (indirect) origin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the experimental result that blocking AMPA receptors prevents TMS inhibition.

claim: TMS-evoked activity in L1 neurons was suppressed by CNQX application.
source: Indeed, TMS-evoked activity in L1 neurons was suppressed by CNQX application, significantly reducing the Ca2+ response amplitude by 53 ± 7% (n = 8; p<0.05; Figure 4D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in L1 neurons is of synaptic origin.
source: Therefore, the TMS-evoked Ca2+ response in L1 neurons is of synaptic origin.
evidence: This conclusion is inferred from the observation that CNQX suppresses the TMS-evoked response in L1.

claim: The inhibition of sensory-evoked L5 dendritic Ca2+ responses was primarily mediated by upper-layer inhibitory neurons driven to fire synaptically from neurons or axons recruited by TMS.
source: Taken together, this data suggests that the inhibition of sensory-evoked L5 dendritic Ca2+ responses was primarily mediated by upper-layer inhibitory neurons driven to fire synaptically from neurons or axons recruited by TMS.
evidence: This is a synthesis of multiple experimental observations including CNQX effects and laminar profiles.

claim: The generation of a magnetic field is most likely to evoke firing in cell bodies as opposed to dendrites or axons.
source: A recent combined experimental and theoretical investigation of the biophysical underpinnings of TMS suggested that the generation of a magnetic field is most likely to evoke firing in cell bodies as opposed to dendrites or axons (Pashut et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: No dendritic activity was observed with TMS stimulation alone in L5 pyramidal neurons.
source: This is consistent with our finding that no dendritic activity was observed with TMS stimulation alone indicating there was no direct activation of the pyramidal cell dendrites and contrasted with the signals found in both L1 and L2/3 neurons following a TMS pulse.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations reported in the manuscript.

claim: TMS activates neurogliaform interneurons in L1 that target the dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons and suppress Ca2+ activity.
source: It is also consistent with the activation of neurogliaform interneurons in L1 that target the dendrites of L5 pyramidal neurons and suppress Ca2+ activity (Ziemann, 2010; Terao and Ugawa, 2002; Pashut et al., 2011; Tamás et al., 2003; Oláh et al., 2007; Oláh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to previous work on neurogliaform interneurons.

claim: Dendritic inhibition arises from the metabotropic inactivation of L-type (Cav1) channels in the apical dendrite.
source: This form of dendritic inhibition arises from the metabotropic inactivation of L-type (Cav1) channels in the apical dendrite that underlie the dendritic Ca2+ activity (Wozny and Williams, 2011) and can last several hundred milliseconds (Pérez-Garci et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The suppression of Ca2+ channels can significantly reduce the action potential firing of the pyramidal neuron even when the driving input to the pyramidal neuron is not predominantly dendritic.
source: The suppression of Ca2+ channels can significantly reduce the action potential firing of the pyramidal neuron even when the driving input to the pyramidal neuron is not predominantly dendritic (Palmer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The similarity of some of the effects of TMS to interhemispheric inhibition has been noted previously in human studies.
source: The similarity of some of the effects of TMS to interhemispheric inhibition has been noted previously in human studies (Jiang et al., 2013; Lee, 2014; Pérez-Garci et al., 2013; Ferbert et al., 1992) including its mediation via GABAB receptor-activation (Ferbert et al., 1992; Kobayashi et al., 2003), although these investigations could not examine the cellular mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work in humans.

claim: Interhemispheric inhibition is mediated via GABAB receptor-activation.
source: The similarity of some of the effects of TMS to interhemispheric inhibition has been noted previously in human studies (Jiang et al., 2013; Lee, 2014; Pérez-Garci et al., 2013; Ferbert et al., 1992) including its mediation via GABAB receptor-activation (Ferbert et al., 1992; Kobayashi et al., 2003), although these investigations could not examine the cellular mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The effect on dendritic Ca2+ was the same for both large and small TMS coils.
source: For this study, we used a large coil typically used in humans and a smaller (25 mm) coil designed for use in rodents. The effect on dendritic Ca2+ was the same in both cases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different coil sizes.

claim: The cortical feedback fibers which synapse onto the tuft dendrites of pyramidal neurons are located in the part of the cortex closest to the magnetic coil (i.e. L1) in both rats and humans.
source: However, the cortical feedback fibers which synapse onto the tuft dendrites of pyramidal neurons are located in the part of the cortex closest to the magnetic coil (i.e. L1) in both rats and humans (Larkum et al., 1999; Larkum, 2013), suggesting there would be overlap with respect to the influence of TMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work on cortical anatomy.

claim: Cell assemblies over different cortical regions might be associated through the activation of dendritic Ca2+ spikes in L5 neurons.
source: We were interested in this, in particular, because we have previously hypothesized that cell assemblies over different cortical regions might be associated through the activation of dendritic Ca2+ spikes in these neurons (Larkum, 2013).
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dendritic activity in L5 neurons is a marker of important cognitive processes.
source: According to this hypothesis, dendritic activity in these neurons is a marker of important cognitive processes.
evidence: This is presented as part of a hypothesis about dendritic function.

claim: TMS has been used to alleviate some of the symptoms of hemispatial neglect via unknown inhibitory processes.
source: For instance, TMS has been used to alleviate some of the symptoms of hemispatial neglect (Nyffeler et al., 2009) and auditory hallucinations (Giesel et al., 2012) via unknown inhibitory processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical work.

claim: TMS has been used to alleviate auditory hallucinations via unknown inhibitory processes.
source: For instance, TMS has been used to alleviate some of the symptoms of hemispatial neglect (Nyffeler et al., 2009) and auditory hallucinations (Giesel et al., 2012) via unknown inhibitory processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical work.

claim: The inhibitory actions of TMS is due to the recruitment of upper cortical layer interneurons mediating both GABAA and GABAB-receptor-activated inhibition in the dendrites of pyramidal neurons.
source: In conclusion, the results presented here indicate that the inhibitory actions of TMS is due to the recruitment of upper cortical layer interneurons mediating both GABAA and GABAB-receptor-activated inhibition in the dendrites of pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: Male or female Wistar rats (P30-P40) were used in these experiments.
source: Male or female Wistar rats (P30-P40) were used in these experiments.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental subjects.

claim: Urethane (intraperitoneal, 1.5 g/kg) was used for experiments under anesthesia.
source: Urethane (intraperitoneal, 1.5 g/kg) was used for experiments under anesthesia, according to the guidelines of the Federal Veterinary Office of Switzerland and LAGeSo Berlin.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the anesthesia protocol.

claim: Large dendritic Ca2+ responses to brief hindpaw stimulation (100 V, 1 ms) were reliably evoked after 70 min loading with OGB1 AM.
source: Using this approach, large dendritic Ca2+ responses to brief hindpaw stimulation (100 V, 1 ms) were reliably evoked after 70 min loading with OGB1 AM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological observation about the timing required for indicator loading.

claim: The lateral spread of locally injected drug was approximately 300 μm.
source: (B) The lateral spread of the dye was approximately 300 μm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental measurements using fluorescent dye shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cortical application of fluorophores penetrates the cortex to layer 2/3.
source: (F) Therefore, cortical application of fluorophores penetrates the cortex to layer 2/3.
evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental measurements of dye penetration shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: TMS did not significantly influence the dendritic response to hindpaw stimulation when evoked greater than 100 ms before hindpaw stimulation.
source: Compared to control (TMS 50 ms before HS) which causes a 45 ± 5% decrease in the evoked dendritic Ca2+ response to HS (see Figure 1; solid; n=17), on average, TMS did not significantly influence the dendritic response to HS when evoked greater than 100 ms before HS (lines; n=6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing timing-dependent effects of TMS.

claim: There was no significant difference between the TMS evoked inhibition using either the small (25 mm) or large (70 mm) TMS coil.
source: There was no significant difference between the TMS evoked inhibition of the HS dendritic response using either the small (25 mm; n=10) or large (70 mm; n=7) TMS coil.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different coil sizes.

claim: There was no significant difference between the TMS evoked inhibition using either airpuff or electrical hindpaw stimulation.
source: There was no significant difference between the TMS evoked inhibition of the HS dendritic response using either hindpaw stimulation technique.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different stimulation methods.

claim: There was no excitatory Ca2+ response to TMS in layer 5 dendrites.
source: (A) Ca2+ transients in a population of layer 5 pyramidal neuron dendrites during TMS delivered at increasing strengths (50%, 80%, 90%, 100% ). Note, there was no excitatory Ca2+ response to TMS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The 'flat' periscope was able to capture the same Ca2+ responses as the 'vertical' periscope.
source: In this configuration, the 'flat' periscope was able to capture the same Ca2+ responses as the 'vertical' periscope.
evidence: This is a methodological validation supported by experimental comparison.

claim: TTX application into layer 5 caused a dramatic increase in L5 dendritic Ca2+ responses to hindpaw stimulation using both the 'flat' periscope and the 'vertical' periscope.
source: As previously reported by (Murayama et al., 2009), TTX application into L5 caused a dramatic increase in L5 dendritic Ca2+ responses to hindpaw stimulation using both the 'flat' periscope and the 'vertical' periscope (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to previous work.

claim: The electric field produced by TMS should be approximately 150-200 V/m.
source: Given this experimental design, the electric field should be approximately ~150–200 V/m (Cohen et al., 1990) magnetic stimulation is comparatively indifferent to the conductive properties of the skull (Wagner et al., 2006), and since the small (3 × 4.4 mm) craniotomy is therefore unlikely to change the currents produced by the coil.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the experimental setup and supported by citations.

claim: Magnetic stimulation is comparatively indifferent to the conductive properties of the skull.
source: Given this experimental design, the electric field should be approximately ~150–200 V/m (Cohen et al., 1990) magnetic stimulation is comparatively indifferent to the conductive properties of the skull (Wagner et al., 2006), and since the small (3 × 4.4 mm) craniotomy is therefore unlikely to change the currents produced by the coil.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: There was no behavioral response of the rat during TMS.
source: Further, there was no behavioral response of the rat during TMS and increasing TMS strength did not elicit an excitatory response in layer 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the behavioral effects of TMS.

claim: Increasing TMS strength did not elicit an excitatory response in layer 5.
source: Further, there was no behavioral response of the rat during TMS and increasing TMS strength did not elicit an excitatory response in layer 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.
